title: Meeting Lester Young and his family in Minneapolis
summary: Thomas recalls dance work around the Twin Cities and meeting Prez, his father and brother Lee, then seeing Lester with King Oliver in Kansas City and finding him scared of New York.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: It doesn't (?) to anything. So going back to Minneapolis...

So Minneapolis... I stayed with a good family in Minneapolis. And I played in this little band. We played all over town. We played all the big dances. Because one of the dance halls was right on my side of the town where we lived. And then we played for dances in St. Paul.
And I got to meet so many good musicians. Now, that's where I first met Prez. Prez came... They... Evidently...
Yes. The carnival played in Minneapolis, but evidently the carnival broke up. And the father had the band...
Prez's father, yeah. And I got to meet his brother, too. I met him, and he...

Lee. Lee was younger than Prez. And it's a funny thing. Lee and I became great friends through the years, but Prez always seemed... He called me Joe. I never did understand that. But you know, I didn't read much into it. Because I remember one time I saw Lester in Kansas City, and he was playing with the master...one of the masters...King Oliver. He was playing in King Oliver's band.
He did? Lester played with King Oliver?

Yeah. And I was talking to him, and he said, 'Man, I'm scared...' He was scared to come to New York. I said, 'Man, you got to be crazy. You ain't got no trouble in New York.' Because I knew how much he could play. Because boy, he played the heck out of the alto, and then he changed to tenor. See, he was really originally an alto player, and then he changed to tenor, but he had that New Orleans background in him, and he just had it.
You know, there's something about Prez that a lot of people don't know. To me, on the tenor, he was the most melodic of all the Jazz saxophone players. When he played a
theme, you could remember the theme. A lot of his solos even you can remember because they were melodic.

He was just a melodic guy. And I remember I met him in Kansas City, and he was...I got to talking to him, and he was scared to come to New York. I told him, "You ain't got nothin' to worry about in New York," because I know he... He played so much better than I did.
